claim: Doxorubicin is widely used for the treatment of breast cancer, bladder cancer, lymphomas, and acute lymphocytic leukemia.
source: The chemotherapeutic drug, doxorubicin, is widely used for the treatment of breast cancer, bladder cancer, lymphomas, and acute lymphocytic leukemia (Smith et al., 2010; Jang et al., 2023; Geffen and Man, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Smith et al., 2010; Jang et al., 2023; Geffen and Man, 2002).

claim: Doxorubicin improves the survival rate of cancer patients.
source: Despite its success in improving the survival rate of cancer patients, doxorubicin causes serious adverse effects, including cardiomyopathy, bone marrow suppression, hair loss, and skeletal manifestations (Cardinale et al., 2015; Tacar et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cardinale et al., 2015; Tacar et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2013).

claim: Doxorubicin causes serious adverse effects, including cardiomyopathy, bone marrow suppression, hair loss, and skeletal manifestations.
source: Despite its success in improving the survival rate of cancer patients, doxorubicin causes serious adverse effects, including cardiomyopathy, bone marrow suppression, hair loss, and skeletal manifestations (Cardinale et al., 2015; Tacar et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cardinale et al., 2015; Tacar et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2013).

claim: Bone complications of doxorubicin include osteoporosis, a metabolic disease characterized by decreased bone mass and deteriorated microarchitecture.
source: Bone complications include osteoporosis, a metabolic disease that is characterized by decreased bone mass and deteriorated microarchitecture, and associated with increased risks for the development of late fractures, and morbidities in the elderly populations (Cauley and Lui, 2009; Cawthon et al., 2009; Cawthon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cauley and Lui, 2009; Cawthon et al., 2009; Cawthon et al., 2012).

claim: 20–50% of geriatric patients (≥65 years) with a hip fracture die within 1 year of fracture.
source: In fact, it was reported that 20–50% of geriatric patients (≥65 years) with a hip fracture die within 1 year of fracture (Coleman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Coleman et al., 2013).

claim: Doxorubicin causes bone loss by promoting osteoclastogenesis while suppressing osteoblastogenesis.
source: Consistent with the dogma that bone resorption by osteoclasts (OCs) and bone formation by osteoblasts is uncoupled in osteoporotic patients, doxorubicin causes bone loss by promoting osteoclastogenesis while suppressing osteoblastogenesis (Yao et al., 2020; Chai et al., 2014; Rana et al., 2013; Zhou and Kuai, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Yao et al., 2020; Chai et al., 2014; Rana et al., 2013; Zhou and Kuai, 2020).

claim: Increased production of senescence-associated secretory phenotype, enhanced generation of reactive oxygen species, and dysregulated autophagy and mitochondrial metabolism are proposed mechanisms of doxorubicin-induced bone pathology.
source: Increased production of senescence-associated secretory phenotype, enhanced generation of reactive oxygen species, and dysregulated autophagy and mitochondrial metabolism are proposed mechanisms of doxorubicin-induced bone pathology (Yao et al., 2020; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Yao et al., 2020; Park et al., 2022).

claim: Doxorubicin intercalates into DNA thereby impeding the activity of DNA repair enzymes such as topoisomerase II and impairing DNA replication.
source: Doxorubicin intercalates into DNA thereby impeding the activity of DNA repair enzymes such as topoisomerase II and impairing DNA replication (Robson et al., 1987; Lawrence, 1988; Bonner and Lawrence, 1990; Abe et al., 2022; Tewey et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Robson et al., 1987; Lawrence, 1988; Bonner and Lawrence, 1990; Abe et al., 2022; Tewey et al., 1984).

claim: Defective DNA repair culminates in genomic instability and cell demise, events that can provoke uncontrollable release of intracellular contents such as DNA and various danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
source: Defective DNA repair ultimately culminates in genomic instability and cell demise, events that can provoke uncontrollable release of intracellular contents such as DNA and various danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about DNA damage and cell death.

claim: NETs are web-like structures in which DNA is decorated with peptides, some of which have anti-microbial and inflammatory properties.
source: DNA-enriched entities include neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), web-like structures in which DNA is decorated with peptides, some of which have anti-microbial and inflammatory properties (Komada et al., 2018; Apel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Komada et al., 2018; Apel et al., 2021).

claim: NETs can propagate inflammation following their engulfment by phagocytes.
source: NETs can also propagate inflammation following their engulfment by phagocytes (Boccia et al., 2022; Blayney and Schwartzberg, 2022; Nakazawa et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boccia et al., 2022; Blayney and Schwartzberg, 2022; Nakazawa et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2021).

claim: DNA in the cytoplasm is detected by DNA sensors, including absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), and cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate synthase, which can trigger immune responses aimed at eliminating the mislocated DNA.
source: Since DNA normally resides in the nucleus and mitochondria, its presence in the cytoplasm is detected by DNA sensors, including absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), and cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate synthase, which can trigger immune responses aimed at eliminating the mislocated DNA (Sun et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Rathinam et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Sun et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Rathinam et al., 2010).

claim: Oxidized DNA and various DAMPs can be sensed by NLRP3.
source: Oxidized DNA and various DAMPs can also be sensed by NLRP3 (Shimada et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2014; Xian et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Shimada et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2014; Xian et al., 2022).

claim: Upon recognition of DAMPs or PAMPs, AIM2 and NLRP3 assemble protein platforms comprising the adaptor protein ASC and caspase-1.
source: Upon recognition of DAMPs or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), AIM2 and NLRP3 assemble protein platforms comprising the adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC) and caspase-1.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about inflammasome assembly.

claim: Inflammasomes are responsible for the maturation of pro-interleukin-1β (pro-IL-1β) and pro-IL-18 to IL-1β and IL-18, respectively.
source: These protein complexes known as inflammasomes are responsible for the maturation of pro-interleukin-1β (pro-IL-1β) and pro-IL-18 to IL-1β and IL-18, respectively (Guo et al., 2015; Sharma and Kanneganti, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Guo et al., 2015; Sharma and Kanneganti, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: Inflammasome-comprising caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD), generating N-terminal fragments, which form IL-1β- and IL-18-secreting conduits, and cause the inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis.
source: Inflammasome-comprising caspase-1 also cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD), generating N-terminal fragments, which form IL-1β- and IL-18-secreting conduits, and cause the inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis (Guo et al., 2015; Sharma and Kanneganti, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Guo et al., 2015; Sharma and Kanneganti, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: Chronic or excessive stimulation of inflammasomes can cause disease.
source: While acute activation of inflammasomes is important for the clearance of the perceived danger and restoration of homeostasis, chronic or excessive stimulation of these safeguard mechanisms can cause disease.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about inflammasome function.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of NLRP3 cause skeletal abnormalities in humans.
source: Gain-of-function mutations of NLRP3 cause skeletal abnormalities in humans (Aksentijevich et al., 2002; Feldmann et al., 2002), which are reproduced to a great extent in knock-in mice expressing NLRP3 harboring mutations found in these patients (Bonar et al., 2012; Qu et al., 2015; Snouwaert et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Aksentijevich et al., 2002; Feldmann et al., 2002; Bonar et al., 2012; Qu et al., 2015; Snouwaert et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: Degraded bone matrix components, which are released during bone resorption, promote inflammasome activation and OC differentiation.
source: In normal mice, degraded bone matrix components, which are released during bone resorption, promote inflammasome activation and OC differentiation (Alippe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Alippe et al., 2017).

claim: Age-associated bone loss has been linked to chronic low-grade inflammation mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Age-associated bone loss has also been linked to chronic low-grade inflammation mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome (Youm et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Youm et al., 2013).

claim: Radiation causes bone loss through GSDMD downstream of AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes, but not NLRC4 inflammasome.
source: More relevant to this study, radiation, which is also used as an anti-neoplastic therapy, causes bone loss through GSDMD downstream of AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes, but not NLR family caspase recruitment domain containing protein 4 (NLRC4) inflammasome (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Xiao et al., 2020).

claim: Doxorubicin caused massive bone loss in wild-type mice.
source: Doxorubicin, but not the vehicle, caused bone loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D). Doxorubicin also caused bone loss in 10-week-old WT male mice, a response that was associated with increased OC number and surface (Figure 1A–E) and decreased bone formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Doxorubicin-induced bone loss was associated with increased osteoclast number and surface.
source: Doxorubicin also caused bone loss in 10-week-old WT male mice, a response that was associated with increased OC number and surface (Figure 1A–E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: Doxorubicin-induced bone loss was associated with decreased bone formation.
source: Doxorubicin also caused bone loss in 10-week-old WT male mice, a response that was associated with increased OC number and surface (Figure 1A–E) and decreased bone formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Doxorubicin inflicted bone damage independently of sex.
source: Since doxorubicin inflicted bone damage independently of the sex, afterward mechanistic studies focused mainly on male mice and revolved around innate immune responses, which regulate OC-mediated bone resorption in pathological conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both male and female mice showed bone loss in response to doxorubicin.

claim: WT mice exposed to doxorubicin for 3 days exhibited higher serum levels of IL-1β, IL-18, IL-6, and TNF-α compared to vehicle-injected counterparts.
source: Accordingly, WT mice exposed to doxorubicin for 3 days exhibited higher serum levels of IL-1β, IL-18, IL-6, and TNF-α compared to vehicle-injected counterparts (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Levels of inflammatory cytokines inversely correlated with the abundance of white blood cells.
source: Levels of these inflammatory cytokines inversely correlated with the abundance of white blood cells (WBCs; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Doxorubicin lowered the number of circulating lymphocytes and monocytes.
source: While doxorubicin lowered the number of circulating lymphocytes and monocytes, the number of neutrophils, the most abundant immune cells in the blood, increased 2 hr post-drug exposure before progressively returning to baseline levels.
evidence: Inferred from the data on white blood cell counts.

claim: The number of neutrophils increased 2 hr post-doxorubicin exposure before progressively returning to baseline levels.
source: While doxorubicin lowered the number of circulating lymphocytes and monocytes, the number of neutrophils, the most abundant immune cells in the blood, increased 2 hr post-drug exposure before progressively returning to baseline levels.
evidence: Inferred from the data on white blood cell counts.

claim: Levels of ATP were higher in doxorubicin-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated cohorts.
source: Consistent with the leukopenic outcome, levels of ATP, which is released by dead cells, were higher in doxorubicin-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated cohorts (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Doxorubicin induced NET formation as evidenced by increased levels of citrullinated histone 3 (Cit-H3), myeloperoxidase (MPO), and cell-free DNA (cfDNA).
source: We found that doxorubicin induced NET formation as evidenced by increased levels of citrullinated histone 3 (Cit-H3; Figure 2G), myeloperoxidase (MPO; Figure 2H), and cell-free DNA (cfDNA) (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: Doxorubicin did not induce IL-1β secretion by BMMs within its reported potent concentrations (1.5–12 µM) without LPS priming.
source: Within its reported potent concentrations (1.5–12 µM) (Saleh et al., 2021; Eljack et al., 2022), doxorubicin did not induce IL-1β secretion, but it significantly caused the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; Figure 3A and B), a marker of cell death as it is released only upon plasma membrane rupture (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Doxorubicin significantly caused the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) by BMMs.
source: Within its reported potent concentrations (1.5–12 µM) (Saleh et al., 2021; Eljack et al., 2022), doxorubicin did not induce IL-1β secretion, but it significantly caused the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; Figure 3A and B), a marker of cell death as it is released only upon plasma membrane rupture (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Doxorubicin promoted IL-1β and LDH release by LPS-primed BMMs in a dose-dependent fashion, with the maximal effect on IL-1β secretion achieved at 6 µM.
source: By contrast, doxorubicin promoted IL-1β and LDH release by LPS-primed BMMs in a dose-dependent fashion, with the maximal effect on IL-1β secretion achieved at 6 µM (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LPS attenuated LDH release induced by low doxorubicin concentrations (1.5 and 3 µM).
source: Unexpectedly, LPS attenuated LDH release induced by low doxorubicin concentrations (1. 5 and 3 µM) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ATP levels were higher in the supernatants of doxorubicin-treated BMMs compared to controls, a response that was further enhanced by LPS.
source: ATP levels were higher in the supernatants of doxorubicin-treated BMMs compared to controls, a response that was further enhanced by LPS (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LPS induced ASC speck formation only in the presence of nigericin.
source: As anticipated, LPS induced ASC speck formation only in the presence of nigericin, a well-known trigger of NLRP3 inflammasome assembly signals (Figure 3D, E, and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E, and H.

claim: Doxorubicin induced ASC speck formation only in LPS-primed BMMs.
source: Likewise, doxorubicin induced ASC speck formation only in LPS-primed BMMs (Figure 3F, G, and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F, G, and H.

claim: Levels of caspase-1 (p10) and GSDMD (p30) fragments were higher in cells treated with LPS+doxorubicin compared to doxorubicin alone.
source: Levels of caspase-1 (p10) and GSDMD (p30) fragments, which are generated upon inflammasome activation, were higher in cells treated with LPS+doxorubicin compared to doxorubicin alone (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSDMD (p10) and GSDME (p35) fragment abundance was comparable between cells exposed to LPS+doxorubicin and doxorubicin alone.
source: GSDMD (p10) and GSDME (p35) fragments, which are proteolytically generated by caspase-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), were also detected, but their abundance was comparable between cells exposed to LPS+doxorubicin and doxorubicin alone (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Doxorubicin activates both caspase-1 and caspase-3, which cleave GSDMD and GSDME, ultimately causing pyroptosis and IL-1β release.
source: Together, these results suggest that doxorubicin activates both caspase-1 and caspase-3, which cleave GSDMD and GSDME, ultimately, causing pyroptosis and IL-1β release.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on caspase and gasdermin cleavage.

claim: Incubation of mouse bone marrow neutrophils with LPS resulted in increased NLRP3 expression.
source: Incubation of mouse bone marrow neutrophils with LPS resulted in increased NLRP3 expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The abundance of caspase-1 (p10) and GSDMD (p30) was indistinguishable between neutrophils exposed to LPS+doxorubicin and doxorubicin alone.
source: The abundance of caspase-1 (p10) and GSDMD (p30) was indistinguishable between cells exposed to LPS+doxorubicin and doxorubicin alone, likely as the result of cell death as the levels of β-actin used as loading control were markedly reduced in samples from these cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: LPS induced IL-1β secretion by neutrophils, a response that was enhanced by doxorubicin in a dose-dependent manner.
source: LPS also induced IL-1β secretion, a response that was enhanced by doxorubicin in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: LPS reduced baseline as well as doxorubicin-induced LDH release by neutrophils.
source: LPS reduced baseline as well as doxorubicin-induced LDH release (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cit-H3 and MPO were detected in neutrophils treated with doxorubicin but not with vehicle.
source: Consistent with in vivo results, Cit-H3 and MPO were detected in cells treated with doxorubicin but not with vehicle (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Levels of cfDNA were higher in doxorubicin-exposed cultures compared to untreated or cultures treated with LPS.
source: Accordingly, levels of cfDNA were higher in doxorubicin-exposed cultures compared to untreated or cultures treated with LPS (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: IL-1β levels were higher in cells treated with LPS and doxorubicin compared to LPS, an outcome that was inhibited by DNase I.
source: IL-1β levels were higher in cells treated with LPS and doxorubicin compared to LPS, an outcome that was inhibited by DNase I (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LPS induction of IL-1β and LDH release by BMMs required doxorubicin, a response that was significantly reduced in Aim2-/- or Nlrp3-/- cells.
source: LPS induction of IL-1β and LDH release by BMMs required doxorubicin, a response that was significantly reduced in Aim2-/- or Nlrp3-/- cells (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: LPS induced IL-1β secretion by neutrophils, an outcome that was enhanced by doxorubicin, and comparably attenuated in all mutants.
source: LPS induced IL-1β secretion by neutrophils, an outcome that was enhanced by doxorubicin, and comparably attenuated in all mutants (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Administration of doxorubicin to WT mice caused bone loss associated with increased OC number and surface.
source: Administration of doxorubicin to WT mice caused bone loss associated with increased OC number and surface (Figure 7E–I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with the results shown above (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E-I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Doxorubicin-induced bone loss responses were reduced slightly in Nlrp3-deficient mice, but significantly in Aim2 null mice.
source: These responses were reduced slightly in Nlrp3-deficient mice, but significantly in Aim2 null mice.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of bone loss data across different genotypes.

claim: Aim2-/- male mice lost bone comparably to Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- and casp1-/- counterparts.
source: Aim2-/- male mice lost bone comparably to Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- and casp1-/- counterparts (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Similar trends in bone changes were observed in female mice, though Aim2-/- mice were more osteopenic than casp1-/- mice.
source: Similar trends in bone changes were observed in female mice, though Aim2-/- mice were more osteopenic than casp1-/- mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: The AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes participate to various extent in doxorubicin bone-damaging effects.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that the AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes participate to various extent in doxorubicin bone-damaging effects.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of AIM2 and NLRP3 deficiency on bone loss.

claim: Inflammasome-independent actions of doxorubicin on bone are not negligible.
source: They also suggest that inflammasome-independent actions of this drug on bone are not negligible.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bone loss persists in inflammasome-deficient mice.

claim: The AIM2 inflammasome and the NLRP3 inflammasome to a lesser extent played an important role in bone-damaging effects of doxorubicin.
source: We found that the AIM2 inflammasome and the NLRP3 inflammasome to a lesser extent played an important role in bone-damaging effects of doxorubicin.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of AIM2 and NLRP3 deficiency on bone loss.

claim: The comparable bone phenotype of Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- and casp1-/- mice suggested that the AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes were the primary mediators of doxorubicin actions.
source: The comparable bone phenotype of Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- and casp1-/- mice suggested that the AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes were the primary mediators of doxorubicin actions.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of bone phenotypes across different genotypes.

claim: Residual doxorubicin-induced bone loss was higher in Aim2-/- and Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- female mice than in male counterparts.
source: The interplay among these pathways may have accounted for the sex differences in the bone outcomes of inflammasome insufficiency as residual doxorubicin-induced bone loss was higher in Aim2-/- and Aim2-/-;Nlrp3-/- female mice than in male counterparts.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of bone loss data between male and female mice.

claim: Sexual dimorphic actions of inflammasomes were not unprecedented as uneven severity of atherosclerosis was found in male and female Nlrp3-deficient mice with gonadal insufficiency.
source: Sexual dimorphic actions of inflammasomes were not unprecedented as uneven severity of atherosclerosis was found in male and female Nlrp3-deficient mice with gonadal insufficiency (Chen et al., 2020) and sex-dependent differential activation of AIM2 and NLRP3 inflammasomes in macrophages from systemic lupus erythematous had been reported (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2015).

claim: Doxorubicin causes neutropenia, lymphopenia, and anemia in patients.
source: Doxorubicin causes neutropenia, lymphopenia, and anemia in patients (Gatti et al., 2018; Boccia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Gatti et al., 2018; Boccia et al., 2022).

claim: Administration of doxorubicin to mice caused leukopenia, which correlated with lymphocytopenia and monocytopenia.
source: Consistent with the clinical situation, administration of doxorubicin to mice caused leukopenia, which correlated with lymphocytopenia and monocytopenia, and was associated with fluctuations in neutrophil counts.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on white blood cell counts.

claim: The transient neutrophilic effects of doxorubicin in mice may be the result of emergency granulopoiesis.
source: Since neutrophils were highly sensitive to the cytotoxic effects of doxorubicin, the transient neutrophilic effects of this drug in mice may be the result of emergency granulopoiesis, a physiological response that is rapidly triggered to restore adequate neutrophil number.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed neutrophil dynamics.

claim: Doxorubicin activated the effectors of apoptosis, pyroptosis, and NETosis, including caspase-1, caspase-3, GSDMD, and GSDME.
source: This leukopenic outcome was consistent with increased serum levels of cell death-associated DAMPS (ATP and cfDNA) and our results showing that doxorubicin activated the effectors of apoptosis, pyroptosis, and NETosis, including caspase-1, caspase-3, GSDMD, and GSDME.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on caspase and gasdermin activation.

claim: Pyroptosis and NETosis accounted for the cytokinemic effects of doxorubicin.
source: Since pyroptosis and NETosis promote inflammation and immune responses, we argued that they accounted for the cytokinemic effects of doxorubicin.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on cytokine levels and cell death mechanisms.

claim: Other studies found that doxorubicin reduced NET formation in cancer models and by human neutrophils in vitro.
source: Other studies, however, found that doxorubicin reduced NET formation in cancer models and by human neutrophils in vitro (Lu et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Lu et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2019).

claim: The discrepancy in NET formation findings may be due to differences in the experimental models and cell context-dependent actions of doxorubicin.
source: This discrepancy may be due to differences in the experimental models and cell context-dependent actions of doxorubicin.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain conflicting findings in the literature.

claim: A correlation exists between the levels of extracellular DNA and IL-1β.
source: This view was consistent with our data showing a correlation between the levels of extracellular DNA and IL-1β as well as by the inhibition of IL-1β secretion by DNase I.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on cfDNA and IL-1β levels.

claim: Doxorubicin activated the NLRP3 inflammasome and induced the release of ATP.
source: We also found that doxorubicin activated the NLRP3 inflammasome and induced the release of ATP, a well-known activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on NLRP3 activation and ATP release.

claim: Whether doxorubicin activated the NLRP3 inflammasome directly by perturbing the plasma membrane or indirectly via generation of secondary signals such as ATP remained unclear.
source: Whether doxorubicin activated the NLRP3 inflammasome directly by perturbing the plasma membrane or indirectly via generation of secondary signals such as ATP remained unclear.
evidence: Acknowledgment of uncertainty regarding the mechanism of NLRP3 activation.

claim: Inflammasomes are key players in bone loss caused by doxorubicin.
source: By showing that inflammasomes are key players in bone loss caused by doxorubicin, this work advances our knowledge on potential mechanisms of action of this drug on this tissue (Figure 8).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that inflammasome deficiency attenuates bone loss.
